doc.title: Jane Bunnett interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 25, 2024

title: Where her compositions come from: influences and piano versus horn
summary: She is influenced by everything, especially Don Pullen and others, and writes at either piano or horn, much during Covid.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Let me ask you about your composing process. There’s a couple of things that I really like about it, partly in the category of orchestration with the unison vocal and the soprano © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-
sax. And also unison string bass and left hand piano on occasion. Where do your compositions come from? Are you inspired by anything in particular?

Pretty much everything. I know that’s sort of a typical question, but that’s a hard question Monk, because I think like I mean I just feel like I’m influenced by so many things that I just hear, particular pieces like Pharoah Sanders and Leon Thomas, “The Creator Has a Master Plan.” I think of that, I think of Duke Ellington “Money Jungle.” I think of McCoy Tyner — what’s it called that tune? “Fly with the Wind.” I think of Don Pullen especially, you know his music, which had a huge effect on me. Carla Bley — like everything. Everything. Everything — I just find everything informs me really, to be honest.
Do you go to the piano first?

I sort of go between the two. Sometimes it’ll start with the piano. Sometimes it might start just with the horn noodling like on the last record, you know, and that was sort of a lot of the music was written during Covid, I would just be sitting up in nature with my horn and I’d just start playing a line and so a seed of an idea came and I’m just — you know work for that sort of maybe for an hour or so and then maybe later in the day go down to the piano and say oh let’s see if I can figure out a bass — what am I — where is this going? So I go between the two things. Might start on the piano, might start on the horn.
